classification_signals: The present paper critically reviews biophilic design patterns and identifies their main shortcomings. (p. 2, Abstract)

Finally, adaptive building envelopes are presented as a hypothetical solution to optimize the biophilic qualities of buildings and address the biological needs of people living and working in extreme cold climates in northern territories. (p. 2, Abstract)
Moreover, the study is conducted based on a critical review of knowledge in biophilic design, photobiology, and lighting design. (p. 3, Introduction)
This paper calls special attention to building envelopes and adaptation strategies as a promising hypothesis to address the challenges of biophilic design for northern regions. (p. 15, Section 6)
Finally, the paper identifies the promising hypothesis of adaptive building envelopes. (p. 17, Conclusion)
title: A photobiological approach to biophilic design in extreme climates

limitations: Lack of recommendations applicable to extreme cold climates for biophilic design.
Lack of adaptation to local photoperiods in biophilic design.
Lack of a systemic framework integrated into the design process for biophilic design.
Existing lighting standards mainly developed for image-forming demands, neglecting non-image-forming effects and biophilic design.
Lack of effective and practical models to actively consider and evaluate circadian effects of light in a space.
No guideline offered to adapt light in the built environment for alertness and performance increase.
Biophilic design qualities not yet defined as an index, indicator, or rating system.
Proposed assessment methods and indexes for biophilic design are still far from being comprehensively, productively, and efficiently involved in the design process or post-occupancy evaluation.
No investigation regarding the efficiency of adaptive envelopes in extreme cold climates and their improvement of human NIF responses.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper proposes a photobiological approach to biophilic design, particularly for extreme cold climates, to address challenges related to human well-being and environmental conditions. It critically reviews existing biophilic design patterns and lighting standards, highlighting shortcomings such as the lack of adaptation to extreme cold climates, local photoperiods, and integration into a systemic design framework. Key findings emphasize the importance of non-image-forming effects of light on human circadian rhythms, alertness, and health, advocating for a revision of lighting standards to incorporate these effects and biophilic principles. The paper hypothesizes that adaptive building envelopes could optimize biophilic qualities and fulfill the photobiological needs of people in northern territories. Limitations include the absence of practical guidelines, assessment systems for biophilic quality, and empirical studies on adaptive envelopes in extreme cold climates.
